The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career and Mentorship
podcast.body: Rock was a top employee and assistant producer at Bruce Fairbairn's Little Mountain Sound studio, where he developed into Fairbairn's protégé. He initially performed longer than Fairbairn, working with Paul Hyde into the late 1980s. "But he also had an assistant producer job at Little Mountain Sound with Bruce and he became so good at his job that he became sort of Bruce's protégé."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Independent Production Success
podcast.body: After becoming Bruce Fairbairn's protégé, Bob Rock began taking on his own clients, and his production resume grew to include a wide array of notable artists. "Eventually, Bob started taking on his own clients and now his resume reads like some kind of who's who."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Maui Residency
podcast.body: Bob Rock has been residing in Maui for the past nine years, where he operates his own recording studio. "Bob Rock has been living in Maui for the last nine years where he operates his own recording studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Production Philosophy for Metallica
podcast.body: For Metallica's "Black Album," Bob Rock advocated for a streamlined sound, focusing on traditional song structures and melody, and reducing the intensity of riffing, drumming, and thrashing. This approach led to a significant increase in album sales despite initial backlash from purist fans. "Bob made them work with traditional song structures. He made them concentrate more on melody. He got them to pull back on the riffing and the drumming and the thrashing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vancouver Music Scene Origins
podcast.body: Bob Rock emerged from the Vancouver music scene, similar to Bruce Fairbairn. "Bob also came out of the Vancouver music scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Cult Band" Status Pre-Black Album
xref.body: Before collaborating with Bob Rock on "The Black Album," Metallica was described as a "cult band," albeit a "big cult band," consistently selling at least two million copies per record. "See before Bob came along, Metallica was doing all right, but they were really just a cult band. Okay, they were a big cult band. Each record sold at least two million copies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Battle of Bands Win Led to Bob Rock's First Ever Production Credit
xref.body: The band started as the K-Tels in 1978 in Vancouver but were threatened with legal action by the cheap record company K-tel International and renamed themselves Young Canadians. Frontman Art Bergman would remain a presence in Canadian alt-rock for decades, ultimately being made a Member of the Order of Canada in 2020. The band won a local Battle of the Bands contest that awarded them studio time at a new facility called Little Mountain Sound. The engineer assigned to these unknown contest winners was a young man named Bob Rock — it was the first time Rock ever produced anything. He went on to produce Metallica, Mötley Crüe, Bon Jovi, The Cult, the Tragically Hip, and many others. "The engineer assigned to them was some kid named Bob Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: From Assistant to Producer
xref.body: Malcolm Burn was an assistant at Grand Avenue Studios and was later hired by Daniel Lanois to run Kingsway Studios in New Orleans. Like Bruce Fairbairn and Bob Rock, he transitioned from a band member (Boys Brigade) into full-time production. "And one of the guys he hired to run the place was an assistant at Grand Avenue named Malcolm Bern. Malcolm used to be in a band-2 they were called Boys Brigade but like Bruce Fairburn and Bob Rock Malcolm eventually got into producing full-time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mentor to Bob Rock
xref.body: Bruce Fairbairn mentored Bob Rock, who started as an assistant producer at Fairbairn's Little Mountain Sound studio and later became his protégé. "Eventually, Bob started taking on his own clients and now his resume reads like some kind of who's who. ... And he got to where he is today thanks to the guidance and mentoring he received from another Canadian Superproducer, the late Bruce Fairburn."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producer Sells Stake in Black Album
xref.body: Bob Rock, who produced Metallica's "Black Album," sold his royalty stake from that record. "Bob Rock, for example, sold his stake in Metallica's black album. He was getting royalties from that and he sold them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Purist Reaction to "The Black Album"
xref.body: Metallica purists reacted negatively to the streamlined sound introduced by Bob Rock on "The Black Album." "And of course Metallica purist freaked out at the result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shift from Raw Speed to Polished Sound
xref.body: Before "The Black Album," Metallica was known for "raw speed and raw power." However, with the 1991 album, producer Bob Rock guided them to "slow down a bit and polished up their sound," a move that angered speed metal purists but significantly broadened their appeal. "Now up until this record, Metallica was all about raw speed and raw power."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transformative Impact of Bob Rock
xref.body: Bob Rock believed Metallica was "one of music's best kept secrets" and convinced them to alter their sound for "The Black Album," leading to an exponential increase in sales from two million to twenty million records. "But Bob believed that they were one of music's best kept secrets. He convinced them to change their sound for what became known as the Black Album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
